section.title: Ruth Gleans in Boaz's Field
section.sectionRationale: The second act is a single day in a barley field that changes everything. Ruth goes out to glean and happens onto the field of Boaz, a worthy kinsman, who shows her extraordinary favor and protection. Naomi recognizes God's hand and names Boaz as one of their kinsman-redeemers. It is one movement introducing the redeemer and turning Naomi's bitterness toward hope.
section.thesis: As a poor foreign widow gleans for survival, the hidden providence of God guides her to the field of a worthy redeemer whose lavish kindness begins to fill the empty and reveals that the LORD has not withdrawn His loving devotion from the living or the dead.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Ruth sets out to glean and happens onto Boaz's field; Boaz notices and blesses her; his lavish provision at mealtime; and Naomi's discovery that Boaz is a kinsman-redeemer.

units.label: Ruth happens onto Boaz's field
units.note: the providence of a chance meeting

verses.text: Now Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a prominent man of {{chayil|noble character}} from the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.
And Ruth the Moabitess said to Naomi, “Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight I may find {{chen|favor}}.” “Go ahead, my daughter,” Naomi replied.
So Ruth departed and went out into the field and {{laqat|gleaned}} after the harvesters. And she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech.

units.label: Boaz notices and blesses Ruth
units.note: under whose wings you have taken refuge

verses.text: Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and said to the harvesters, “The LORD be with you.” “The LORD bless you,” they replied.
And Boaz asked the foreman of his harvesters, “Whose young woman is this?”
The foreman answered, “She is the Moabitess who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab.
She has said, ‘Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the harvesters.’ So she came out and has continued from morning until now, except that she rested a short time in the shelter.”
Then Boaz said to Ruth, “Listen, my daughter. Do not go and glean in another field, and do not go away from this place, but stay here close to my servant girls.

Let your eyes be on the field they are harvesting, and follow along after these girls. Indeed, I have ordered the young men not to touch you. And when you are thirsty, go and drink from the jars the young men have filled.”
At this, she fell on her face, bowing low to the ground, and said to him, “Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner?”

Boaz replied, “I have been made fully aware of all you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, how you left your father and mother and the land of your birth, and how you came to a people you did not know before.
May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose {{kanaph|wings}} you have taken refuge.”
“My lord,” she said, “may I continue to find favor in your eyes, for you have comforted and spoken kindly to your maidservant, though I am not like one of your servant girls.”

units.label: Lavish provision at the meal
units.note: she ate and was satisfied and had some left over

verses.text: At mealtime Boaz said to her, “Come over here; have some bread and dip it into the vinegar sauce.” So she sat down beside the harvesters, and he offered her roasted grain, and she ate and was satisfied and had some left over.
When Ruth got up to glean, Boaz ordered his young men, “Even if she gathers among the sheaves, do not insult her.
Rather, pull out for her some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her to gather. Do not rebuke her.”
So Ruth gathered grain in the field until evening. And when she beat out what she had gleaned, it was about an ephah of barley.

units.label: Naomi recognizes a kinsman-redeemer
units.note: the LORD has not withdrawn His kindness

verses.text: She picked up the grain and went into the town, where her mother-in-law saw what she had gleaned. And she brought out what she had saved from her meal and gave it to Naomi.

Then her mother-in-law asked her, “Where did you glean today, and where did you work? Blessed be the man who noticed you.” So she told her mother-in-law where she had worked. “The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz,” she said.

Then Naomi said to her daughter-in-law, “May he be blessed by the LORD, who has not withdrawn His {{chesed|kindness}} from the living or the dead.” Naomi continued, “The man is a close relative. He is one of our {{goel|kinsman-redeemers}}.”
Then Ruth the Moabitess said, “He also told me, ‘Stay with my young men until they have finished gathering all my harvest.’”
And Naomi said to her daughter-in-law Ruth, “My daughter, it is good for you to work with his young women, so that nothing will happen to you in another field.”
So Ruth stayed close to the servant girls of Boaz to glean grain until the barley and wheat harvests were finished. And she lived with her mother-in-law.

chayil.gloss: Strength, worth, valor, or noble character. Boaz is introduced as a gibbor chayil, a man of standing and moral weight, not merely wealth. The same phrase, eshet chayil, crowns Ruth in 3:11 and the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31:10; the book deliberately pairs a worthy man with a worthy woman whom God brings together.

chen.gloss: Favor, grace, undeserved kindness. Ruth hopes to glean behind someone in whose sight she may find favor, and marvels that she, a foreigner, has found it. The word quietly points to grace, kindness shown to one who has no claim on it, which is exactly how Boaz treats her and how God treats sinners.

laqat.gloss: To glean, gather, or pick up. The law commanded landowners to leave the edges of their fields and any dropped grain for the poor, the widow, and the foreigner to gather, Leviticus 19:9-10 and Deuteronomy 24:19-21. Ruth is precisely the person the gleaning laws were meant to protect, and Boaz obeys the law with overflowing generosity.

kanaph.gloss: Wing, edge, or corner of a garment. Boaz blesses Ruth for taking refuge under the wings of the God of Israel. In 3:9 Ruth will ask Boaz to spread the corner of his garment, the same word, over her; what Boaz prays that God will do, God answers through Boaz himself, who becomes the very refuge he blessed.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast love, loyal covenant kindness. Naomi sees Boaz's generosity as evidence that the LORD has not withdrawn His chesed from the living or the dead. It is the great theme of Ruth, and here it turns Naomi's bitterness toward hope as she recognizes God's faithful hand.

goel.gloss: Kinsman-redeemer or guardian-redeemer, a near relative legally responsible to rescue a family member in need: to buy back sold land, redeem a relative from slavery, and raise up a name for the dead. The BSB footnote points to Leviticus 25:25-55. Naomi's naming of Boaz as one of their redeemers is the hinge of the plot and a shadow of Christ, our Redeemer.

basic.context: To keep herself and Naomi alive, Ruth goes out to glean, gathering leftover grain that the law reserved for the poor. By what looks like chance she ends up in a field owned by Boaz, a well-off and godly relative of her dead father-in-law. Boaz has heard of her loyalty to Naomi, and he protects her, feeds her, and orders his men to leave extra grain for her. When Ruth tells Naomi, Naomi realizes Boaz is a kinsman-redeemer, and her hope begins to revive.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative packed with quiet theology. The word happened in verse 3 is deliberate understatement: what looks like luck is really God's providence. Boaz is held up as a model of generosity and integrity, and Naomi's response teaches us to read good gifts as evidence of God's steadfast love. The gleaning laws show God's heart for the poor and the outsider.
basic.originalLanguages: Boaz is a man of chayil, worth and noble character; Ruth hopes for chen, favor or grace, and keeps finding it. She comes under the kanaph, the wings, of God for refuge, the same word she will use of Boaz's garment in chapter three. Naomi sees God's chesed, loving devotion, at work and names Boaz a goel, a kinsman-redeemer.
basic.typology: Boaz the kinsman-redeemer is the clearest picture in the book of Christ our Redeemer: a worthy relative who has the right, the means, and the willing heart to rescue the helpless. His welcome of a foreign widow and his covering of her point to the way Christ receives sinners and outsiders under His wings.
basic.christ: Boaz foreshadows Jesus, the true and better kinsman-redeemer, who takes on our flesh to become our near relative, pays the full price, and rescues the poor and the outsider. Ruth taking refuge under God's wings is answered when Christ gathers His people as a hen gathers her chicks, and the abundant grain that satisfies her points to the fullness we find in Him.
basic.god: God's providence quietly governs the whole day, guiding Ruth to the right field at the right time. We learn that God cares for the poor, the widow, and the foreigner, that He works through ordinary means and generous people, and that His loving devotion has not been withdrawn even when His people feel empty.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 24 command the gleaning that provides for Ruth. Psalm 91 speaks of refuge under God's wings. And Boaz as redeemer looks ahead to Christ the Redeemer in Titus 2 and 1 Peter 1.
basic.oneStory: The story of redemption advances as God guides an empty widow to a worthy redeemer. Boaz's kindness begins to reverse Naomi's emptiness and introduces the office of kinsman-redeemer that the whole book, and finally the gospel, is about. It all points to Jesus, who redeems the poor and the outsider and covers them with His love.

context.literary: The chapter is framed by two conversations with Naomi, Ruth asking permission to glean in verse 2 and Ruth reporting the day's events in verses 19 to 22, so that everything Boaz does happens inside a single day bracketed by domestic dialogue at either end. The narrator's understated she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, verse 3, doubles the same root for chance in the underlying Hebrew, an emphatic construction that all but announces its own irony, since the narrator has already told readers in verse 1 that Boaz is a relative of Naomi's, information Ruth herself does not yet have. The scene then unfolds in escalating stages of favor: Boaz first orders his men merely to leave Ruth unmolested, verse 9, then invites her to eat at his own table, verse 14, then instructs the harvesters to pull grain deliberately from the bundles for her, verse 16, each stage more generous than the last, so that by evening an ephah of barley, far more than ordinary gleaning would yield, has accumulated almost as a structural proof of the escalation. Naomi's closing exclamation, blessed be the man who noticed you, and her naming of Boaz as a kinsman-redeemer turns the whole day's providence into a formal, legal category the rest of the book will now pursue.
context.historical: Gleaning functioned as Israel's closest approach to a welfare system: Leviticus 19:9-10 and Deuteronomy 24:19-21 required landowners to leave the edges of a field unharvested and any dropped or forgotten sheaves behind for the poor, the orphan, the widow, and the foreigner, a legal minimum Boaz will be shown exceeding rather than merely meeting. A young widow gleaning alone among male harvesters, especially a foreign one, faced real danger of harassment or worse, which is precisely why Boaz's specific order that the young men not touch her, verse 9, and his warning against insult in verse 15, carry more weight than polite formality; he is naming and forbidding a known risk. Fields at this period were harvested by cutting with a sickle and binding into sheaves, with reapers moving in a line behind which gleaners like Ruth would follow closely, so that Boaz's instruction to stay close to his own servant girls placed Ruth under a kind of informal protective custody for the length of the harvest. An ephah, roughly twenty dry quarts or about twenty-nine pounds, was a substantial haul for a single day's gleaning, likely representing several weeks of ordinary bread for two women, a detail the original audience, familiar with such measures, would have recognized instantly as remarkable generosity rather than routine charity.
context.canonical: The office of kinsman-redeemer that Naomi names in verse 20 is rooted in Leviticus 25:25, where a near relative may redeem property or a person sold into servitude to keep it within the family, and in the levirate custom of Deuteronomy 25:5-10, which the rest of the book will show Boaz fulfilling in a more voluntary, generous form than the law strictly required of him, since he is not in fact the nearest of the family's redeemers, 4:1-4. This chapter's language of refuge under God's wings, verse 12, echoes the Psalter's own picture of the LORD covering His people with feathers, Psalm 91:4, and will return in Ruth's own mouth in 3:9, when she asks Boaz to spread his garment, the same word for wing, over her, so that what Boaz prays God will do for Ruth here, he himself becomes the answer to two chapters later. The whole scene also sits inside the book's larger argument about outsiders: the same law that excluded Moabites from Israel's assembly, Deuteronomy 23:3-6, is here being fulfilled toward a Moabite by a righteous Israelite landowner exceeding its minimums, so that law and grace operate together rather than in competition. Centuries later this same chapter's vocabulary, redeemer, refuge, reward, will resurface across the New Testament's own account of a greater redemption, Titus 2:14, 1 Peter 1:18-19, Galatians 4:4-5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The narrator wants readers to hold two things together without letting either cancel the other: Ruth's own diligence, she asks permission to glean, she works from morning until evening with only a short rest, verse 7, and God's hidden providence, she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz. Neither is presented as the whole explanation; the chapter refuses the false choice between human effort and divine sovereignty that readers are often tempted to force onto stories like this. Equally important is the author's portrait of Boaz as a standard against which every reader of the book, then and now, might measure covenant faithfulness in practice, not simply pious speech but concrete provision, protection, and public blessing spoken over a vulnerable outsider. Naomi's transformation across the chapter, from a woman with nothing to say about God in chapter one's closing lament to a woman blessing the LORD by name in verse 20, is the author's clearest signal that this ordinary day of gleaning is the turning point the whole book has been building toward.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter describes what happened on one exceptional day; it does not legislate that every landowner must match Boaz's generosity to the letter, though it plainly commends the spirit behind it. The gleaning laws themselves, by contrast, are genuinely prescriptive, standing commands about how a harvest is to be gathered so that the poor are provided for, and Boaz's conduct functions as a worked example of a command kept generously rather than grudgingly. Ruth's diligence is likewise held up for admiration rather than issued as a formula guaranteeing that hard work will always attract a wealthy protector; the book nowhere promises every gleaner a Boaz. What does transfer directly into every reader's life is the pattern underneath the particulars, honest labor offered without any promise of reward, met by a providence that is real even when it is invisible until, as here, someone finally names it out loud.

debates.question: How should we read the word happened in verse 3, that Ruth chanced onto Boaz's field?

views.label: Deliberate irony pointing to providence
views.case: The narrator uses the language of chance precisely to make the reader smile and look higher: there are no accidents in God's ordering of events, and the whole book insists that the LORD is quietly steering everything toward redemption.

views.label: Ordinary means under God's rule
views.case: Ruth made a free, sensible choice to glean, and God worked through that ordinary decision; the point is not that Ruth was passive but that God governs even our everyday steps.

debates.bearing: Both readings land on the same truth: what looks like coincidence is the fingerprint of God's providence, which does not cancel human action but works through it.

debates.question: What makes Boaz a model of godly character here?

views.label: Covenant-shaped generosity
views.case: Boaz goes far beyond the letter of the gleaning law, ordering extra grain left for Ruth, feeding her at his table, and guarding her honor, embodying the chesed the law was meant to produce.

views.label: Faith expressed in blessing and protection
views.case: His speech is saturated with the LORD, he blesses Ruth in God's name, and he protects the vulnerable outsider, showing a faith that works itself out in tangible kindness.

debates.bearing: Either emphasis presents Boaz as a picture of righteous love that anticipates Christ, the Redeemer whose generosity and protection know no limit.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3's she happened to come doubles the same Hebrew root for chance in a single clause, an emphatic construction that draws attention to itself precisely where the narrator wants readers to suspect the opposite of pure accident; Boaz has already been introduced in verse 1 as Naomi's relative, information the narrator shares with the reader but withholds from Ruth, so that what looks like luck to her looks, to anyone paying attention, like the working out of a plan already in motion.

Laqat, to glean, names a technical, legally protected activity, not casual scavenging. Leviticus 19:9-10 and Deuteronomy 24:19-21 command landowners to leave field edges and dropped grain precisely so that gleaners like Ruth have a right, not merely a charity, to what they gather; Boaz's later orders to his young men, deliberately pull out some stalks from the bundles and leave them for her, verse 16, take a legal minimum and multiply it into overflowing kindness.

Chayil, describing Boaz in verse 1 as a man of standing, carries a semantic range wide enough to cover military valor, wealth, and moral worth all at once, which is exactly why the same word crowns Ruth herself in 3:11, a woman of noble character, and why it names the excellent wife of Proverbs 31:10. The book deliberately pairs a chayil man with a chayil woman, letting readers see before either of them does that they are cut from matching cloth.

Chen, favor, is the word Ruth hopes to find in someone's eyes, verse 2, and it recurs at verse 10 and verse 13 as she marvels at receiving it despite being a foreigner; chen names undeserved kindness given to someone with no claim on the giver, exactly the kind of favor that later theology calls grace, unearned and freely given rather than purchased by status or merit.

Kanaph, wing, is what Boaz invokes when he blesses Ruth for taking refuge under the wings of the God of Israel, verse 12, an image drawn from the same picture of divine shelter in Psalm 91:4, and Ruth will use the identical word in 3:9 to ask Boaz himself to spread the corner of his garment, kanaph again, over her; the prayer Boaz prays for Ruth here he himself becomes the answer to two chapters later, without either of them planning it that way.

Goel, kinsman-redeemer, names a legally defined role rooted in Leviticus 25:25, a near relative obligated, though never forced, to rescue family land, family members, or a family's name from loss. Remarkably, this same consonantal name, Boaz, later names one of the two bronze pillars Solomon sets at the entrance to the temple, 1 Kings 7:21, though Scripture nowhere explains why the name was reused, a small and unexplained echo rather than a claimed pattern.

typology.fulfillment: A kinsman-redeemer under the law had to meet three conditions at once, near relation by blood, the legal right to redeem, and the willingness to actually do it, and Boaz alone among Naomi's relatives combines all three in generous measure, going further than the law strictly required, 4:1-6. Christ meets the same three conditions in a deeper key: He becomes our near kinsman by taking on flesh and blood, Hebrews 2:14, holds the right to redeem as the sinless one alone qualified, and freely wills to pay the price Himself rather than waiting to be asked. The type falls short only in the currency of the payment, barley and land against Boaz's name, His own blood against ours, Titus 2:14, 1 Peter 1:18-19.

typology.type: Ruth taking refuge under the wings of the LORD
typology.fulfillment: Boaz blesses Ruth for having come to take refuge under the wings of the God of Israel, language borrowed from the Psalter's picture of divine shelter, Psalm 91:4, before Ruth has any settled place to call her own in Israel. Jesus later takes up the same image and applies it to Himself directly, longing to gather Jerusalem's children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, Matthew 23:37, showing that the shelter Boaz merely invokes in prayer, Christ offers in person, even to those, like Jerusalem in that moment, who refuse it. The type escalates here because the sheltering God of Israel and the sheltering Christ turn out to be the same one, seeking refuge for outsiders long before any of them ask for it.

typology.type: The abundant grain that satisfies and overflows
typology.fulfillment: Ruth eats until she is satisfied and still has grain left over, verse 14, and gleans by evening an ephah of barley, far beyond what a single gleaner could expect, a small harvest of overflow inside a chapter otherwise about survival. Jesus later feeds five thousand from five loaves and two fish with twelve baskets left over, John 6:1-13, and calls Himself the bread of life whom no one who comes to Him will ever hunger, John 6:35, taking the pattern of provision that merely satisfies in Boaz's field and turning it into a promise that satisfies forever. Ruth's leftover grain fed two women for a season; the bread of life feeds all who come to Him without ever running out.

study.christ:
Boaz asks who this young woman is before Ruth has done anything to earn his attention, verse 5, initiative that runs entirely one direction, from the man with standing toward the outsider with none. This is the shape of grace throughout the gospel: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, Luke 19:10, and God demonstrates His own love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, Romans 5:8, love that moves toward the needy before the needy have done anything to deserve the attention. Ruth marvels at exactly this reversal, why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner, verse 10, a question every believer eventually asks in one form or another.

There is also a quiet lesson in how Boaz answers his own prayer. He asks the LORD to give Ruth a full reward for her kindness to Naomi, under whose wings she has taken refuge, verse 12, and then spends the rest of the chapter, and the rest of the book, becoming that very reward himself, feeding her, protecting her, and eventually marrying her. God's care for His people rarely stays abstract for long; it tends to arrive wearing a face, provision embodied rather than merely promised, the same logic that reaches its fullest expression when God does not simply send help to His people from a distance but takes on flesh and comes among them Himself, John 1:14.

Ruth's diligence, gleaning from morning until evening with only a short rest, verse 7, is real and is genuinely rewarded, yet nothing in the chapter suggests she earned Boaz's notice by her labor rather than received it as an unlooked-for gift layered on top of it. That balance, honest effort held together with undeserved favor, previews the New Testament's own insistence that believers work out their salvation while it is God who works in them both to will and to act, Philippians 2:12-13, grace and effort operating together rather than competing for credit.
study.god:
An ordinary greeting exchanged between Boaz and his harvesters, the LORD be with you, the LORD bless you, verse 4, shows a whole working field where the LORD's name is simply assumed background language, not reserved for temple or festival. This is what it looks like when a nation's ordinary life, not only its official worship, has been shaped by the character of its God, a God who legislated margins into private property, requiring landowners to leave field edges and dropped grain for the poor, the orphan, the widow, and the foreigner, precisely because He Himself executes justice for the fatherless and the widow and loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing, Deuteronomy 10:18. The gleaning law is not incidental charity legislation; it is God's own priorities written into the economics of the land.

Naomi's declaration in verse 20, that the LORD has not withdrawn His chesed from the living or the dead, marks the theological turning point of the book. In chapter one she could only name God as the source of her affliction; here, watching an ephah of barley and hearing Boaz's name, she recognizes that the same LORD she accused has in fact never stopped being kind, to Elimelech's memory as much as to herself and Ruth in the present. This is not God changing His mind about Naomi; it is Naomi's sight finally catching up to what had been true all along.

The chapter also displays God's providence operating without a single reported miracle, no voice from heaven, no supernatural sign, only a field, a harvest, a generous man, and a hardworking widow. This is how God ordinarily governs His world, through people, through law, through the unremarkable rhythms of planting and reaping, and readers are meant to take this as normal rather than disappointing; the absence of spectacle is not the absence of God. The LORD who commanded gleaning laws centuries earlier is the same LORD quietly making sure, on this particular day, that those laws land on exactly the field and the woman they were written to protect.

crossReferences.note: The law commands that harvesters not reap all the way to a field's edge nor gather every fallen grape or grain, but leave it for the poor and the foreigner. Ruth gleans in Boaz's field entirely on the strength of this command, a right written into Israel's law long before she was born, not a favor Boaz invents on the spot.

Sheaves forgotten in the field, and grain, olives, or grapes left after the first pass, belong by law to the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. Ruth fits every category this law names at once, a foreigner and a widow, and the command anticipates exactly her situation generations before she is ever introduced.

The psalm pictures the LORD covering His own with feathers, a refuge under His wings. Boaz applies this very image to Ruth in verse 12, praying that the God of Israel, under whose wings she has come for refuge, would reward her, borrowing Israel's own worship language to bless an outsider newly arrived among His people.

Because those God rescues share in flesh and blood, the Son too shared in the same, so that through death He might break the power of the one who holds death, and become a merciful and faithful high priest. Boaz, a flesh and blood relative willing to redeem, previews exactly this kind of near, costly kinship.

If a poor Israelite must sell his property, his nearest relative may redeem it and keep it in the family. This is the precise legal category Naomi has in mind when she names Boaz a kinsman-redeemer in verse 20, a role about land and family name that the rest of the book will show Boaz fulfilling.

God executes justice for the fatherless and the widow, and loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing. Boaz's provision for Ruth, a foreign widow, enacts this description of God's own character in one afternoon of ordinary harvest work, law and character meeting in a single generous man.

Jesus states His mission plainly, to seek and to save what was lost. Boaz's initiative toward Ruth, asking who she is before she asks anything of him, mirrors in miniature the same seeking love that moves toward the needy before they have done anything to deserve the attention.

Jesus laments over Jerusalem, longing to gather her children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings. The same wing imagery Boaz uses to bless Ruth in verse 12 becomes, in Christ's own mouth, a picture of His own longing to shelter His people, even those who will not come.

Jesus calls Himself the bread of life, promising that whoever comes to Him will never hunger. Ruth eats until she is satisfied with bread and grain left over in Boaz's field, verse 14, a foretaste, on a much smaller scale, of the fullness Christ offers to everyone who comes to Him.

Boaz will later tell Ruth that all his fellow townspeople know she is a woman of noble character, the same Hebrew phrase used of Boaz himself in 2:1. The book pairs a worthy man and a worthy woman, letting the same word describe them both before their story is finished.

A nearer relative than Boaz is offered the chance to redeem Elimelech's land and marry Ruth first, and he declines. Boaz's willingness in this chapter to go beyond the law's bare minimum for Ruth becomes, two chapters later, an actual legal redemption completed at the town gate before witnesses.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God gave every seed-bearing plant across the whole earth for food, Genesis 1:29, provision without scarcity built into creation's very design. Genesis 3 broke that ease, thorns and thistles now contesting every harvest, bread earned only by the sweat of a cursed ground, Genesis 3:17-19. Boaz's field, in one afternoon, becomes a small, deliberate rollback of that curse: grain left standing on purpose for the poor, stalks pulled out by design rather than accident, a harvest generous enough that a foreign widow eats until satisfied and still carries home more than she can immediately use. Nothing here undoes the fall on a cosmic scale, but it enacts, in miniature, exactly the kind of world the fall took away, ground yielding more than enough, freely shared rather than fiercely guarded.

This is also redemption's story gathering momentum. Naomi named the LORD as her accuser in chapter one; by this chapter's end she is naming Him the source of unbroken kindness, and naming a specific man as the legal means through which that kindness will keep working, a kinsman-redeemer who can restore what death and famine took. The law that protected gleaners like Ruth and the law that authorized redeemers like Boaz turn out to be two arms of the same divine intention, provision for the poor and restoration for the lost, working together rather than in tension.

The chapter ends still short of the wedding it is quietly building toward, but Scripture's own ending supplies the picture this harvest field only gestures at, a marriage supper where the Lamb's bride has made herself ready, Revelation 19:9, and where the tree of life yields its fruit continually for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. A gleaner's single ephah of barley and a redeemer's spoken blessing are small, ordinary things, and Scripture's whole method is to hide its grandest promises inside exactly such small, ordinary things until the day they are fully unwrapped.

sermon.title: Favor to the Humble
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Ruth, this message expounds Ruth 2:4-13, the meeting of Boaz and Ruth in the field, his kindness to the foreign widow, and her refuge under the wings of the God of Israel. A clear, orthodox handling of the heart of this movement.

quiz.q: How did Ruth end up gleaning in the field of Boaz?

options.text: She happened onto his field while gleaning, an ordinary event that the narrator hints was God's providence.
options.note: Ruth 2:3 says she happened to come to Boaz's field, quiet irony for God's guiding hand.

options.text: Naomi arranged in advance for her to work for Boaz.
options.note: Naomi only recognized Boaz afterward; Ruth came to his field before either planned it.

options.text: Boaz sent servants to bring her to his field.
options.note: Ruth came on her own initiative to glean; Boaz noticed her once she was there.

options.text: She was assigned there by the town elders.
options.note: No official assigned her; she chose to glean and providence did the rest.

quiz.q: How did Boaz treat Ruth in his field?

options.text: He protected her, fed her, and ordered extra grain left for her, going beyond the gleaning law.
options.note: Ruth 2:8-16 shows his lavish, protective generosity to the vulnerable widow.

options.text: He allowed her to glean but kept his distance.
options.note: He did far more than tolerate her; he actively provided for and protected her.

options.text: He warned her not to return the next day.
options.note: The opposite: he urged her to stay in his field for the whole harvest.

options.text: He demanded payment for the grain she gathered.
options.note: He gave freely and generously, asking nothing in return.

quiz.q: What did Boaz say Ruth had done in coming to Israel?

options.text: She had taken refuge under the wings of the LORD, the God of Israel.
options.note: Ruth 2:12 blesses her for seeking refuge under God's wings.

options.text: She had abandoned her duty to her family.
options.note: He praised her loyalty to Naomi, not abandonment; the key image is refuge under God's wings.

options.text: She had come merely to find a wealthy husband.
options.note: Boaz commends her faith and loyalty, not any scheme for wealth.

options.text: She had betrayed the gods of Moab for no reason.
options.note: He honors her turning to the true God as taking refuge under His wings.

quiz.q: What did Naomi realize when she heard the name Boaz?

options.text: That Boaz was a close relative and one of their kinsman-redeemers.
options.note: Ruth 2:20 has Naomi recognize Boaz as a goel, a kinsman-redeemer.

options.text: That Boaz was an enemy to be avoided.
options.note: The opposite: she saw him as a redeemer and a sign of God's kindness.

options.text: That Boaz was a stranger with no connection to them.
options.note: He was in fact a close relative from Elimelech's clan.

options.text: That Boaz intended to take their land unjustly.
options.note: Naomi saw him as a redeemer, evidence of God's steadfast love, not a threat.

quiz.q: How does Boaz point us to Jesus?

options.text: As a worthy kinsman-redeemer who has the right, the means, and the will to rescue the helpless.
options.note: Boaz foreshadows Christ, our near kinsman who redeems the poor and the outsider.

options.text: Only as a kind man with no deeper meaning.
options.note: His kindness is real, but Scripture presents the redeemer role as a picture of Christ.

options.text: As a warning against helping the poor.
options.note: He is a model of generosity, not a warning against it.

options.text: As proof that redemption depends on our own effort.
options.note: Redemption comes through the redeemer's initiative and provision, not the widow's effort.

questions: Ruth stepped out in humble, hard work, and God met her there. Where is God calling you to faithful ordinary effort while trusting Him with the outcome?
What looked like chance was really God's providence guiding Ruth to the right field. Where have you later seen God's hand in what felt like coincidence at the time?
Boaz went far beyond duty to protect and provide for a vulnerable outsider. Who around you is vulnerable or overlooked, and how could you show them that kind of generous kindness?
Ruth took refuge under the wings of the God of Israel. What would it look like for you to run to God for shelter this week rather than to lesser things?
Naomi began to see that God had not withdrawn His steadfast love after all. Where do you need to notice God's kindness reviving hope in a season that has felt empty?

translationNotes.note: A prominent man of noble character renders gibbor chayil, worth and standing; the same root, chayil, describes Ruth in 3:11 and the woman of Proverbs 31:10.
She happened to come to Boaz's field is deliberate understatement; the whole book treats such chance as the working of God's providence.
Wings renders kanaph, which can also mean the corner of a garment; Ruth uses the same word of Boaz's garment in 3:9, so the blessing is answered through Boaz himself.
Kinsman-redeemer renders goel, a legal term for the relative who redeems or vindicates his kin; the BSB footnote points to Leviticus 25:25-55.
